title: 20 mJ, 1 ps Yb:YAG Thin-disk Regenerative Amplifier
protocol: Pump the thin-disk via the coupled fiber at a wavelength of 940 nm by setting the "current" knob on the power supply to 26.2 A, corresponding to the 210-W output, to start lasing in the oscillator in the continuous wave (CW) mode.
Connect a fiber to the spectrometer and place it before the pulse picker after using an appropriate attenuation.
Select the "Spectrometer" tab in the spectrometer software and click "Rescan Devices."
Right-click on the spectrometer name and select "Spectrum Graph."
Click the "Accept" button on the "Choose Target" window.
Block the laser beam and click the "Store Dark Spectrum" button on the tool bar.
Unblock the laser beam to observe the spectrum.
Observe the output power of the CW mode on the power meter before the pulse picker.
Perturb the high-reflectivity mirror inside the laser cavity (on a translation stage) by mechanically pushing the stage from the back.
Observe the spectrum and output power of the pulsed mode before the pulse picker using a spectrometer and a power meter, respectively.
Slightly increase the current on the power supply until a CW spike appears in the spectrum measured by the spectrometer.
Align the hard aperture in the oscillator by tuning its micrometer screws vertically and horizontally to maximize the CW spike.
Observe the depletion of the pump beam profile on the thin-disk.
Run disk camera program and select "Monochrome" from the "choose mode" window.
Click the "Open camera" button on the tool bar to observe the beam spot on the thin-disk.

Tune the piezo linear actuators of the end mirror by pushing the "+" or "-" button on the vertical or horizontal motor from the hand-control pad to align this depletion to the center of the pump beam profile.
Reduce the current on the power supply until the CW spike vanishes in the spectrum.
Repeat steps until a spectrum and an output power similar to reference levels are achieved.
Connect a fast photodiode to an oscilloscope and place it before the pulse picker.
Tune the "trigger level" knob on the oscilloscope to stabilize repeating waveforms.
Observe the output pulse train on the oscilloscope screen.
Select "Peak to Peak Amplitude" from the "Measure" menu to determine pulse-to-pulse stability.
Observe the output beam profile before the pulse picker and determine beam-pointing fluctuations.
Run the beam profiler software and click the "Go, start capture" button.
Open the "beam wander" dialog and click the "clear" button to start new beam-pointing stability measurement.
Measure the pulse duration using frequency-resolved optical gating based on second harmonic generation (SHG-FROG).
Reduce the repetition rate of the oscillator from 11 MHz to 5 kHz by switching the power supply of the pulse picker driver to "on".
Apply high voltage to the crystal.
Select picked pulses from the pulse train using a thin-film polarizer (TFP).
Dump remaining pulses into a beam dump.
Adjust the half-wave plate before the pulse picker to improve contrast.
Pass the picked pulses through the stretcher setup to stretch the pulses to a duration of 2 ns.
Align the picked pulses through the stretcher setup using two mirrors after the pulse picker, if required.
Be aware of all relevant electrical safety regulations before proceeding.
Use appropriate high-voltage isolation.
Remove diagnostics from the beam path.
Turn on the cooling water for the regenerative amplifier.
Switch on the cooling chillers to cool down the pump diodes, thin-disk, laser head, and Pockels cell.
Set the temperature of the chillers to 28 °C, 17 °C, and 18 °C.
Activate the interlock system.
Switch on the power supply of the pump diode unit.
Click the "OUTPUT ON/OFF" button to turn on.
Pump the thin-disk via the coupled fiber at a wavelength of 940 nm by setting the "current" knob to the threshold.
Observe the pump beam profile on the disk using the disk camera.
Select "Circle Geometry" on the "Draw" menu in the disk camera program to mark the position of the beam.
Reduce the power supply current to zero.
Click the "OUTPUT ON/OFF" button to turn off.
Switch off the power supply of the pump diode unit.

Use two mirrors before the regenerative amplifier to align the output beam from the stretcher through the incoupling optics in the regenerative amplifier to reach the first-end mirror (behind the Pockels cell).
Use a beam profiler, an infrared viewer, and a laser viewing card to assist with alignment.
Close the amplifier cavity by turning the quarter-wave plate behind the Pockels cell.
Tune the motorized knobs of the first-end mirror using the "+" or "-" button on driver 1 from the hand-control pad to align the outcoupling beam.
Open the amplifier cavity by turning the quarter-wave plate behind the Pockels cell until maximum laser beam intensity is attained inside the cavity.
Block the back-reflected beam from the second end mirror.
Observe the seed pulses' beam profile on the disk camera program and overlap the beam with the marked position by tuning the knobs of one of the cavity mirrors before the thin-disk.
Unblock the back-reflected beam and observe its spot on the disk camera program.

Tune the motorized knobs of the second end mirror using the "+" or "-" button for the vertical or horizontal motor (driver 2) on the hand-control pad to overlap the back reflection with the marked position.
Observe the switching signal of the Pockels cell with the aid of a fast photodiode.
Set the delay time in the "define delay parameters" dialog box to synchronize the Pockels cell switching and seed pulses.
Set the switching time window to confine one pulse inside the cavity to 4 µs, corresponding to 87 round trips.
Set the internal trigger time to "200 µs" to confine the rate to one pulse every 5 kHz.
Switch on the power supply of the Pockels cell driver and apply high voltage to the crystal.
Switch on the power supply of the pump diode unit and click the "OUTPUT ON/OFF" button.
Set the current knob on the power supply to 57.7 A, corresponding to 280 W, to pump the thin-disk and amplify seed pulses.

Turn the motorized rotation mount of the half-wave plate by pushing the "+" or "-" button on motor A (driver 5) from the hand-control pad to send a few watts of the amplifier output to the compressor.
Compress the laser pulse down to 1 ps by passing the amplified beam through the compressor setup.
Use two mirrors after the regenerative amplifier setup to align the amplified pulses through the compressor setup, if required.
Switch on the power supply of the beam stabilizer unit.
Run the beam stabilizer program on the beam stabilizer computer.
Use two mirrors before the detector setup of the beam stabilizer to align the zero-order diffraction from the first grating in the compressor to the beam stabilizer detectors.
Push the "regulation" button on the beam stabilizer program to lock the laser beam to avoid beam-drift after the compressor.
Turn the motorized half-wave plate again to pass the full output power of the amplifier through the compressor.
Adjust the gain of the beam stabilizer detectors with the aid of a neutral-density filter.
Characterize the time duration of the compressed pulses using SHG-FROG.
Run the program of the beam profiler from the OPCPA computer.
Collimate and adjust the laser beam size after the compressor using an appropriate telescope to reach a peak intensity of 80 GW/cm².
Use the beam profiler, infrared viewer, and laser viewing card.
Guide the fundamental beam (1,030 nm) through a nonlinear crystal (1.5 mm-thick BBO; see Table of Materials, No. 54).
Generate the second harmonic (SH) at 515 nm.
Place a harmonic separator at 45° after the crystal to separate the SH beam from the unconverted fundamental beam.
Tune the knob of the crystal mount to optimize the phase-matching angle of the SH for highest conversion efficiency (70%, corresponding to 70 W).
Observe the power of the SH and the unconverted fundamental beams on the power meters.
Observe the Gaussian beam profile of the SH and the unconverted fundamental beams.
Characterize the temporal shape of the SH pulses using cross-correlation frequency resolved optical gating (XFROG).
